evening.title: India condemns attack on Saudi airport that killed 12, injured over 300
evening.text:
India on Sunday strongly condemned a major attack on Saudi Arabia’s international airport in Riyadh that killed 12 people and injured over 300.
New Delhi said the repeated attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Gulf nation are “completely unacceptable and must cease immediately.” “We strongly condemn the repeated attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport over the past few days, including the dastardly attack on October 10, which have led to loss of lives, injuries and damage to property,” the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said in a statement.
“We express our condolences to the families of the deceased and wish speedy recovery to the injured persons,” it said.
Saudi Arabia has blamed Houthi militants for the attack.
“We stand in solidarity with the people and the government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in defence of their sovereignty, and hope that peace and normalcy returns to the region at the earliest,” the MEA said.

evening.title: OrbitAID Prepares to Demonstrate Satellite Refuelling in Orbit in 2027
evening.text:
OrbitAID is gearing up for an exciting milestone in satellite technology with its upcoming twin satellite launch, AayulSAT-2A and 2B, scheduled for February 2027 aboard an Indian launch vehicle. After their initial AayulSAT-1 mission in early November, which demonstrated internal fuel and power transfer, this new mission aims to showcase advanced capabilities in autonomous satellite servicing.
These 70-kilogram satellites, acting as chaser and target, will be deployed together into Low Earth Orbit before separating. The chaser satellite will then perform precise maneuvers to rendezvous and dock with the target using OrbitAID’s proprietary ARCAS docking system, designed to connect with any satellite’s standard Launch Adapter Ring.
Once docked, the mission will demonstrate two key scenarios: refueling a satellite equipped with OrbitAID’s SIDRP refueling interface and serving as a ‘jetpack’ for satellites without this interface. The robotic arm on the chaser will refuel it first, after which it will boost the target satellite’s orbit to a higher altitude before returning it to its original orbit, completing the mission cycle.
The technologies proven in this mission are stepping stones toward future satellite servicing and refueling operations in Geosynchronous orbit, a sector with immense commercial potential for extending satellite lifespans and enhancing space sustainability.

evening.title: Indian vs Chinese Destroyers: Grim Reapers Simulates Sea Battle and it was a Draw
evening.text:
A naval warfare simulation conducted by YouTube channel Grim Reapers has pitted Indian Navy destroyers against their Chinese counterparts, testing the capabilities of missiles and air-defence systems.
The YouTube channel’s scenario used India’s BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles and Barak-8 surface-to-air missiles against China’s array of YJ-18, YJ-12 anti-ship missiles and the YJ-20 weapon modelled in the game as a high-speed, quasi-hypersonic threat. The creator of the video, which was run in the naval combat game Sea Power , found the Chinese ships to have the overall advantage despite repeated software glitches that affected missile targeting and complicated the results.
India’s Kolkata- and Visakhapatnam-class destroyers fired BrahMos anti-ship missiles in attacks at various engagement ranges. The simulated supersonic missiles’ low-altitude terminal approach was key to the scenarios as China’s layered air-defence systems were tasked in countering the incoming salvo.
India’s Kolkata- and Visakhapatnam-class destroyers carry BrahMos for surface attacks and Barak-8 for air defences. The Indian Ministry of Defence lists both weapons as part of the armament carried by the Visakhapatnam class.
Within the scenarios, China’s Type 052D destroyers used HHQ-9-series missiles and close-in defences while the older Type 052B was represented with HQ-16-series air-defence missiles. The exercises saw a number of intercepted missiles with others able to penetrate the Indian ships’ defences or cause disabling damage.
Grim Reapers used a scenario set at approximately 200 nautical miles where the game used its representation of China’s YJ-20. The creator of the video said the simulated weapon’s impact detection failed to work correctly which required him to count near misses as hits. As such, the outcome of this scenario cannot be seen as a true indicator of the capabilities of either fleet.
The scenario was repeated at a range of approximately 60 nautical miles but without the YJ-20. Indian ships have launched BrahMos missiles while China’s vessels have fired YJ-12 and YJ-18 weapons.
The creator said BrahMos missiles targeted a single Chinese ship despite instructions to split their fire. Chinese air defences intercepted some of the incoming missiles while others got through. One Chinese salvo left an Indian destroyer heavily damaged and unable to fight on.
With anti-ship missiles expended, the scenario saw the remaining vessels closing in for a gunfight with other weapons. The larger main gun of the Chinese ship was the deciding factor in one engagement while a final close-range scenario saw the two vessels ‘double knock out’ each other.
The creator said that Chinese ships won or drew the engagements but noted the issues with the missile targeting, fire distribution and the graphics of the game. The latter is a major limitation as the salvo coordination, target allocation, sensor performance and missile interception rates were all major factors in the outcomes.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE
evening.summary: A naval warfare simulation conducted by YouTube channel Grim Reapers has pitted Indian Navy destroyers against their Chinese counterparts, testing the capabilities of missiles and air-defence systems.

evening.title: DRDO Explores Generative AI to Overcome Battlefield Data Shortage
evening.text:
One of the biggest barriers to integrating artificial intelligence into military systems is not an abundance of algorithms or computing power. It is data. A new paper published in Defence Science Journal describes a DRDO research approach that attempts to address this issue by generating synthetic imagery when sufficiently large real-world datasets are unavailable.
The paper “An Efficient Deep Learning Framework for Accuracy Enhancement of Object Recognition Tasks in Data-Constrained Scenarios Using Synthetic Data Generation – A Futuristic Step Towards AI in Defence”, has been authored by A. Mageswari and S. Sundar. It appears in Volume 76, No. 5 of the journal, published in September 2026, on page 634.
It is of particular relevance to defence, where large, accurately labelled image sets can be challenging to acquire. Military imagery may be sensitive, hard to acquire in sufficient quantity and unevenly distributed across target classes.
The researchers propose a three-stage approach combining generative models, image enhancement and deep-learning-based recognition.
The first stage uses a Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN) to generate synthetic images from a relatively small collection of real images. The objective is to increase the available training materiel without having to collect an appreciably larger amount of real-world image material.
However, the synthetic images generated by the DCGAN can have limited resolution. The second stage therefore makes use of a Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network (SRGAN) to enhance the generated imagery.
The resulting synthetic dataset can then be combined with available real images and used to train an object-recognition model. The study evaluates VGG-based deep-learning architectures alongside other pre-trained convolutional neural networks for their effectiveness for the recognition task.
This approach tackles an issue that is particularly acute in military AI. A commercial computer-vision developer can potentially gather millions of photographs from publicly available sources. A defence organisation dealing with military vehicles, battlefield equipment or other sensitive targets does not have the same flexibility.
The challenge is not simply the number of photographs. AI systems require appropriately labelled and sufficiently varied examples. Rare target classes can be particularly challenging to represent, potentially resulting in class imbalances during training.
Synthetic data presents a potential solution for increasing the diversity of the training set without exposing additional sensitive operational imagery.
The paper is significant in linking a mainstream generative-AI technique to a practical defence requirement: machine-based object recognition when real training data is scarce.
The research is associated with DRDO’s Combat Vehicles Research and Development Establishment (CVRDE), making the work especially relevant to the continued development of computer vision and autonomous capabilities for land systems.
It does not necessarily mean that the study itself demonstrates an operational autonomous combat vehicle, however. It represents a building block for AI-based perception, where a machine must first identify and differentiate objects before more sophisticated autonomous capabilities can be considered.
The research also highlights an important limitation of synthetic-data approaches. Generating more images does not necessarily guarantee better AI. Synthetic images must remain sufficiently representative of real-world objects and environments, while resulting models must be validated against genuine operational imagery.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: Chinese Media Questions AMCA Timeline and Engine Plans
evening.text:
Chinese language commentary has focused sharply on India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme, its development schedule, its reliance on the American GE F414 engine and the challenge of delivering an indigenous fifth-generation fighter amid the expansion of China’s own stealth aircraft fleet.
The debate has sharpened up after reports that India’s first AMCA prototype is set to fly in September 2028. Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh reiterated that that timeline in September 2026, as the government prepared to select an industry partner for prototype development. The programme has been opened to private-sector bidders and Tata Advanced Systems, an L&T-led consortium and a Bharat Forge-led consortium have been shortlisted after technical evaluation.
Chinese commentary has questionedIndia’s capacity to meet that target given that the Tejas fighter has taken far longer to develop than envisioned. Some articles have projected certification around 2032 and service entry in 2034-35 but these later dates should be seen as their projections and not as an official schedule.
One of the sharpest criticisms has centred on the AMCA’s propulsion arrangements. The initial version is expected to employ the GE F414 which is an American turbofan used by the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet. GE lists the engine in the 22,000-pound-thrust class and has agreed to pursue Indian production of F414 engines with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited for the Tejas Mk2 programme.
Chinese commentators have argued that reliance on an imported engine would limit India’s capacity to achieve the performance it is looking for from a fifth-generation fighter, namely sustained supersonic flight without afterburner or supercruise.
The decision to exclude HAL from the shortlist for manufacturing AMCA prototypes has also become a focus of Chinese commentary. Defence Secretary Singh said HAL failed to qualify on what he said were fairly routine technical grounds and not that the government had decided to favour private industry.
The three shortlisted bidders will compete to develop and manufacture the prototypes. Opening the programme to private companies could diversify India’s aerospace manufacturing base but the selected partner will have to demonstrate its capacity to manage a complex fighter development programme that includes stealth structures, flight-control systems, avionics and weapons integration.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: Al-Qaeda Seeks to Expand Its India Network Through Pan-Islamist Strategy
evening.text:
Al-Qaeda is seeking to expand its footprint in India and the subcontinent through its arm Al-Qaeda in the Sub-Continent (AQIS) by promoting a pan-Islamist approach, encouraging Bangladesh-based terror outfits to spawn splinter groups, and building tactical ties with groups across sectarian lines, according to security officials.
AQIS was launched in 2014 with the primary goal of focusing on India and the countries around it. However, the announcement was made at a time when the Islamic State was on top of its game, and this acted as a major deterrent to AQIS’s ambitions.
Security analysts have observed a gradual but potentially dangerous shift in the AQIS strategy, with the outfit increasingly advocating pan-Islamism. The approach seeks to avoid open opposition to any particular sect or sub-sect and instead promote a broader, more inclusive ideological appeal to expand its support base.
An official said that this push being made by Al-Qaeda, especially in the sub-continent, is dangerous.
“AQIS was formed by merging several smaller regional jihadi groups from Bangladesh, Myanmar and India. However, these groups failed to expand significantly despite subscribing to Al-Qaeda’s ideology, largely because of stiff competition from the Islamic State. The latter does not subscribe to the concept of pan-Islamism and opposes various sects and sub-sects, making its approach less inclusive,” the official said.
Another official said that in the sub-continent, Al Qaeda wants to conduct the Africa experiment.
In Africa, where Al-Qaeda has established a strong presence, it avoided declaring war on particular sects and sub-sects. This enabled the outfit to forge closer ties with local groups, which in turn helped strengthen its network across the region.
“Al-Qaeda took a cue from the Islamic State, which committed the mistake of declaring war on every local sect and sub-sect. This shortened the Islamic State’s lifespan as a dominant force and led to its gradual decline in several parts of the world,” the official said.
The focus of Al-Qaeda is currently on the terror groups that are operating out of Bangladesh. The Jammat-ul Mujahideen (JMB) is its biggest ally. The JMB witnessed a split when a faction supported the Islamic State and then went on to become the Neo-JMB.
Al-Qaeda has been encouraging the JMB to create multiple groups such as the Imam Mahmuder Kafila (IMK), which has focused its activities in India.
Al-Qaeda wants groups such as the JMB, Ansarullah Bangla Team (ABT) and Harkat-ul-Jihadi Islami Bangladesh (HuJI-B) to create more splinter groups and ensure that they subscribe only to the ideology that it preaches.
An Intelligence Bureau official said that this suits Al-Qaeda.
“Groups such as the JMB, ABT and HuJI-B already have manpower and operational strength. Al-Qaeda, on the other hand, will continue to act as an ideological mentor to these groups. Further, the creation of these multiple splinter groups will confuse the Indian agencies, while also giving the parent groups the deniability factor,” the official said.
Al-Qaeda feels that it needs to have this pan-Islamist approach. Such a strategy would have a much bigger draw for the outfit.
In the sub-continent, it has decided to create safe havens and also maintain tactical cooperation with Shia groups. These groups, in turn, help Al-Qaeda with both logistical and survival needs, officials say.
Officials said Al-Qaeda is seeking to establish a strong base in India. Its founder, Osama bin Laden, had built the outfit’s doctrine around targeting the ‘far enemy’, a reference to the West.
The outfit now wants to adopt a similar strategy in the subcontinent and has been urging its allies to pursue a more inclusive approach to widen their support base. It is keen to avoid the mistakes made by the Islamic State, which alienated potential allies by targeting various sects and sub-sects.
The Islamic State came with a bang, put on a brutal show, and even captured a wide audience in India. The outfit even radicalised over 20 youths from Kerala and convinced them to join the outfit in Afghanistan.
Many Indians, who had left the country to join the outfit in Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria, immediately became disillusioned.
The Islamic State is extremely violent, and the Indians who joined the outfit complained about discrimination and also about having to do menial jobs.
Al-Qaeda wants to change that and hopes that the inclusive approach that it seeks to take will work wonders for it in the sub-continent, with India being the primary target, an official said.
–IANS–

From Shahed to Geran-5: Lessons India Cannot Ignore
evening.text:
Russia’s evolving Shahed-derived Geran family of drones is drawing attention to a potential capability issue India faces with counter-drone systems: such systems can rapidly become ineffective if the attacking drone speeds through, climbs to altitudes, and employs communications and tactics faster than their own.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, conventional Geran-2-class drones have been intercepted at 90-95% while the interception rate against the newer jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 has dropped to 60%. The former’s increase in speed and altitude have been cited by Ukrainian officials as the principal factor.
This is a significant issue. Shahed/Geran initially threatened to be a relatively slow projectile. The latest iterations threaten to turn the same concept into something increasingly challenging to deal with.
The Geran-4 is said to reach around 500 km/h while the larger Geran-5 can reach 600 km/h and altitudes of up to 6,000 metres. Ukrainian and Western assessments also describe ranges approaching 850-1,000 km for the newer variants.
Ukraine’s many inexpensive interceptor UAVs were designed around Shahed’s slower, propeller-driven predecessors. A target coming at several hundred km/h offers less time for detection, classification, targeting and interception. At higher altitudes, some short-range weapons and machine-gun-based systems also find their performance reduced. Ukraine’s Air Force has specifically pointed these out.
Ukrainian intelligence has also indicated that jet-powered variants can be operated online via mesh communications, enabling an operator to control the drone during its mission. RFE/RL reported that recovered systems included MESH modems that could enable operators to take control over those from Russian or occupied territory.
This adds to the counter-drone challenge. Simply defeating the aircraft may no longer be sufficient. More layers of countermeasures need to be considered such as the navigational, communications, datalinks, satellite positioning, onboard sensing and command architecture of the drone.
Operation Sindoor, as the battle between drones has been dubbed, has demonstrated their value in a high-intensity fight as well as the importance of systems such as counter-drone systems and integrated air defence. However, the experience with the Geran has shown how quickly a manageable target can turn into something substantially more difficult to manage.
It is thus not enough to simply acquire more anti-drone guns, jammers or interceptor UAVs. India has to develop a layered detect-to-engage architecture that can deal with targets having different speeds, altitudes, signatures and levels of autonomy.
Russia’s Geran programme has demonstrated the ability to rapidly evolve a relatively simple platform when given the feedback of the battlefield. Recent assessments described a transition from propeller-driven Gerans to jet-powered variants and an expansion in the production of these as well as the development of new configurations.
That suggests that India, too, has to plan for shorter testing and procurement cycles, modular counter-UAS design and the ability to rapidly introduce new interceptors if the threat evolves.

evening.title: India-Russia Naval Cooperation Gets Fresh Push as INS Sahyadri Reaches Vladivostok
evening.text:
Indian Navy Ship (INS) Sahyadri arrived in Russia’s Vladivostok on Saturday, reaffirming long-lasting friendship and deepening maritime cooperation between the two countries.
“Vladivostok warmly welcomes the Indian Navy ship Sahyadri. A ceremonial welcome by the Russian Navy marked the ship’s arrival in the city, reflecting the spirit of friendship and maritime camaraderie between India and Russia,” the Consulate General of India in Vladivostok posted on X.
INS Sahyadri docked at Vladivostok to participate in the joint Russian-Indian naval exercise INDRA-2026, state-owned Russian television channel Zvezda reported.
The ship’s crew was welcomed at the pier with the traditional bread and salt. Captain First Rank Alexey Ulyanenko, Commander of the Russian Pacific Fleet’s surface ship division, greeted the Indian crew on behalf of the Russian Navy command.
Ulyanenko highlighted the enduring friendly ties between Russian and Indian naval personnel, noting that they continue to grow stronger. The opening ceremony of INDRA-2026 is scheduled for October 13, with the exercise comprising two phases —coastal and sea — to be conducted in the Sea of Japan.
On Thursday, India and Russia reviewed existing military-technical cooperation and discussed co-production and co-development initiatives at the inaugural session of the 24th Working Group meeting of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Military Technical Cooperation and Defence Industry.
“The inaugural session of the 24th Working Group meeting of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Military Technical Cooperation and Defence Industry was held in New Delhi on 08th October 2026,” the Ministry of Defence stated on X.
“The session was co-chaired by Secretary (Defence Production) Shri Sanjeev Kumar from India and First Deputy Director, FSMTC Mr Andrey A. Boytsov, from Russia. Senior officials from both countries joined the deliberations. The discussions were focussed on reviewing existing military-technical cooperation and forging co-production and co-development initiatives to further cement the India – Russia Strategic Partnership in Defence,” it added.
Last week, in a step towards deepening the India-Russia naval partnership, a six-member Russian Navy delegation led by Captain 1st Rank Sergei V Saitov visited the Southern Naval Command and the Indian Naval Academy in Kerala.
Taking to social media platform X, the Indian Navy said that the delegation, during its visit from September 27 to October 1, familiarised itself with the Indian Navy’s overall training architecture, infrastructure and facilities.
“Discussions explored avenues to deepen maritime cooperation, enhance interoperability and further consolidate institutional and professional linkages. A reflection of the enduring naval partnership between India & Russia,” the Indian Navy posted on X.
The visit comes amid continued efforts by India and Russia to strengthen their longstanding defence and strategic ties.
–IANS–

evening.title: Why the IAF Should Build 40 Unmanned Combat Aircraft a Year not run after fighters
evening.text:
Indian Air Force Chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh has said that India needs to induct 36-40 fighter aircraft annually in order to arrest the decline in its fighter squadron strength. This is a valid point in its own right, but it raises an interesting question: instead of trying to get the manned fighter force back to an acceptable size, should India consider pursuing a similar annual target for unmanned combat aircraft?
A parallel target of 30-40 would provide the IAF with more aircraft for reconnaissance, electronic warfare, decoy and strike roles, in addition to manned fighters. The economics change for unmanned combat aircraft. Cutting out the pilot from the equation reduces the cost of sophisticated engines, sensors, avionics, flight-control systems and pilot training, all of which contribute to the high acquisition and operating costs of manned fighters.
Unmanned aircraft offer an alternative route to numbers.
Depending on the size of various kinds of unmanned aircraft, they could serve as a complementary sensor node for jammers, decoys or precision-strike missiles, operating alongside manned fighters, or carry out certain missions where the risk of losing an aircraft is considered acceptable.
The proposed annual target would apply across different classes of unmanned aircraft. While a three-tonne loyal wingman and a 10-tonne stealth UCAV would have very different acquisition costs, payloads and propulsion requirements, they would make up part of an expanded combat-aircraft inventory.
Operation Sindoor has fuelled the debate about unmanned systems, electronic warfare and integrated air-defence systems.
In July 2025, the Chief of Defence Staff General Anil Chauhan called upon the country to develop indigenous UAVs and counter-UAS capabilities, and to have greater domestic capabilities in offensive and defensive technologies. Air Chief Marshal Singh has drawn the correct conclusion from Operation Sindoor: that manned and unmanned systems must work together, and that saturation of drone swarms cannot achieve every military objective.
A future force could utilise unmanned aircraft for extended surveillance, target illumination, electronic warfare and selected precision strikes to help manned aircraft capitalise on opportunities.
Crewed aircraft could take advantage of the “window” created when enemy air-defence systems are suppressed. Unmanned aircraft would have other roles in the suppression of enemy air-defences (SEAD) during the conflict, before the SEAD mission was undertaken (not exclusively afterwards as suggested by some).
India does not have to go from zero to 36; HAL’s CATS Warrior is designed to be a loyal wingman to crewed aircraft, while DRDO’s Ghatak programme targets a larger stealth UCAV capable of more independent operations. The two programmes could form the backbone of an IAF equipped using a “parallel procurement” strategy, with CATS utilising manned-unmanned teaming, and Ghatak filling a different but complementary role to crewed fighters.
HAL’s full-scale Warrior demonstrator has been ground-tested in its engines, with first flight scheduled for 2027, while the SWiFT technology demonstrator of the Ghatak has flown, but the full-scale combat aircraft is still some way off.
A sustained annual production target would give the IAF a clear pathway from demonstrators to combat aircraft fleets, and the opportunity for private manufacturers to develop specialised systems, provided common interfaces and rigorous qualification processes are established. The main challenge would not be in manufacturing airframes, but in developing reliable propulsion, data-link security, autonomous mission software, weapons interface and self-protection against electronic attack.
The IAF would have to evaluate what degree of autonomy would be acceptable, how unmanned aircraft would communicate if links were jammed, and how many aircraft could be controlled effectively by crews.
A large unmanned force, unable to operate effectively in a contested electromagnetic environment, would have limited combat utility. It would be better to set out a phased procurement plan: initially flying operational demonstrators, qualifying multiple designs in different roles, and then moving on to expanded serial production after evaluating costs and performance.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: Show HN: WallHop – 12ft.io is gone, so I built a replacement
evening.text:
Hi HN, I'm Josh. WallHop is a free paywall bypass: paste an article URL (or prefix any URL with wallhop.io/) and you get the readable article without the paywall popup, ads or clutter. No signup, no extension.

I built it after 12ft.io went away. The News Media Alliance took it down in July 2025 and I missed having something I could hit from my phone.

How it works: it started as a fork of everywall/ladder (GPL-3.0) and I've modified it heavily since. Instead of relying on one trick, it chains several bypass methods per request and falls back to archive.is when they all fail, so one site blocking one technique doesn't break it.

Things that might be interesting:

- iOS Shortcut: on iPhone, tap Share > WallHop from any article in Safari or another app. This is how I use it 95% of the time. - It works on Medium member-only posts, which 12ft never handled. - Bookmarklet for desktop, plus /raw/ and /api/ endpoints if you want to script it.

I've tested it against most major news outlets and a bunch of local papers. It won't work everywhere. There are SOME server-side paywalls that are out of reach, and I'd rather say that up front. If you find a site that breaks, I'd love the link, and I can likely figure out a way to bypass it!
